content: Theriac, also known as theriaca, was a complex medicinal preparation that included opium, viper flesh, and a wide variety of other ingredients. It was originally formulated as an antidote to snake venom but later came to be used as a general preventative remedy, or panacea. The term theriac is derived from the Greek word theriaka, which referred to ancient texts about dangerous animals and their bites. Consequently, the antidote for animal bites became known as theriac, which eventually evolved into the English word treacle through Middle English triacle. According to historical accounts, the origins of theriac are linked to King Mithridates VI of Pontus, who conducted experiments with poisons and antidotes on prisoners. Through extensive trials, he claimed to have discovered a universal antidote effective against all venomous reptiles and toxic substances. He combined these antidotes into a single preparation called mithridatium or mithridate. This mixture included opium, myrrh, saffron, ginger, cinnamon, and castor, along with approximately forty other ingredients. After the Romans defeated Mithridates, his medical notes were acquired by Roman physicians, who began to utilize and refine his formulations. The Roman Emperor Nero's physician, Andromachus, enhanced mithridatium by increasing the number of ingredients to sixty-four, incorporating viper flesh as a key component. This improved version was named Theriaca Andromachi or Venice treacle and was particularly esteemed for its efficacy against snakebites. However, by modern standards, this concoction would likely be considered an addictive tranquilizer. Over time, Venice treacle became the standard form of theriac. The renowned Greek physician Galen dedicated an entire book, Theriaké, to the study of theriac. One of his notable patients, the Roman Emperor Marcus Aurelius, reportedly consumed theriac regularly. In 667, ambassadors from the Byzantine Empire (Rûm) presented a theriac preparation to the Emperor of the Tang Dynasty in China. Chinese observers noted that the mixture contained pig gall, was dark red in color, and was held in high regard by the foreigners. The Tang pharmacologist Su Kung documented its reputed effectiveness against a hundred ailments. However, it remains uncertain whether this version of theriac included traditional ingredients such as opium, myrrh, and hemp. The preparation was intended to mature over several years and was prohibitively expensive, making it accessible only to the wealthy. Theriac was used not only for treating bites but also as a preventative measure against poisoning and, eventually, as a remedy for a wide range of conditions. It could be applied as a salve or plaster or consumed in solid chunks. The Theriaca Andromachi or Venice treacle contained sixty-four ingredients, including viper flesh, opium, cinnamon, agarics, and gum arabic. These components were ground into a fine powder and mixed with honey to form an electuary. By the Renaissance, the preparation of theriac had become a formalized and ceremonial process, particularly in Italy. Pharmacists continued to sell theriac as late as 1884.
